# Dynamic Documents with RMarkdown

Every chapter of this course textbook, every assignment you've submitted,
and every chunk of R code you've run so far has lived inside an `.Rmd`
file. This chapter finally explains what that file format actually is,
and teaches you to write one of your own from scratch.

## What is a dynamic document?

A **dynamic document** is a file that combines code, the output of that
code, and narrative writing, all in one place. You're reading one right
now: this entire textbook is written in RMarkdown.

In a dynamic document, code runs live, right inside the document, and
produces "living" output (figures, tables, summary statistics) that
updates automatically whenever the underlying code or data changes. This
is a huge step up from the traditional alternative: running an analysis
in one program, manually copying a figure into a Word document, then
having to redo that copy-paste by hand every time the data changes or you
spot a mistake. A dynamic document never goes out of sync with the code
that produced it, because the two are never separated in the first place.

## Markdown and RMarkdown

Markdown is a lightweight system for formatting plain text, you've been
reading and writing it throughout this course, every chapter of this
book, every `README.md`, every assignment. RMarkdown is a variant of
Markdown built specifically for R: it combines ordinary Markdown text
with embedded, executable R code, and can export the result to many
formats (HTML, PDF, Word documents, slide decks).

The RMarkdown workflow happens in two stages, though you'll never
interact with the intermediate step directly:

1. **Knitting**: the `knitr` package runs every code chunk in your `.Rmd`
   file, captures its output, and weaves the results back into a plain
   Markdown (`.md`) file.
2. **Rendering**: `pandoc` (the same tool underlying this entire course
   textbook) converts that Markdown file into your chosen final format.

Both steps happen automatically when you click "Knit" in RStudio, you
don't need to run them separately.

## Writing an RMarkdown document

### Creating the document

In RStudio, go to **File > New File > R Markdown...**. Give it a title
and select HTML as the output format (the most common choice, and what
we'll use throughout this chapter). RStudio will generate a starter
document with some example content already in it, feel free to delete
everything below the header and start fresh.

#### YAML headers

Every RMarkdown document begins with a **YAML header**: a block between
two lines of three dashes, specifying document-level metadata like the
title, author, date, and output format. YAML stands for "YAML Ain't
Markup Language," a recursive acronym (the "Y" refers to the acronym
itself). It's not actually a markup language like HTML, it's a format
for representing structured data, key-value pairs, lists, nested
settings, in a simple, human-readable way, which is exactly the job it
does here.
```
---
title: "Frog Morphometrics Summary"
author: "Your Name"
date: "2024-06-01"
output: html_document
---
```

You've actually seen this before, every chapter of this textbook (and the
Overview page) has one of these at the top, since bookdown is built on
top of the same RMarkdown system.

### Code chunks

A **code chunk** is a block of R code embedded directly in your document,
set off by three backticks and curly braces containing the language name.

**Try it now:** Create a new RMarkdown document, and add this chunk
anywhere in the body:


<pre><code>&#96;&#96;&#96;{r}
2 + 2
&#96;&#96;&#96;</code></pre>

Knit the document. You should see both the code itself and its output
(`4`) appear in your rendered document.

Every code chunk can take **options**, placed inside the curly braces
after the language name, that control how it behaves. A few you'll use
constantly:

- `echo=FALSE`: runs the code, but hides the code itself from the
  rendered output (only the result shows).
- `eval=FALSE`: shows the code, but doesn't run it (you've seen this
  throughout this textbook, anywhere you weren't meant to run something
  yet).
- `include=FALSE`: runs the code, but hides both the code and its
  output entirely (useful for setup steps, like loading packages, that a
  reader doesn't need to see).
- `fig.width` / `fig.height`: control the size of any plot the chunk
  produces.

### Setting the working directory for all chunks

By default, when you knit a document, every chunk's working directory is
set to the folder the `.Rmd` file itself lives in, not wherever your R
console's working directory happens to be set to at the time. This can
be a source of confusion: a relative path like `"data/frogs.sqlite"`
might work fine when you run a chunk interactively in RStudio, then fail
when you knit the whole document, if your console and your `.Rmd` file
aren't in the same place.

To set a single working directory for every chunk in the document, add a
setup chunk near the very top, right after your YAML header, using
`knitr::opts_knit$set()`:

<pre><code>&#96;&#96;&#96;{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = "/path/to/your/course-repo")
&#96;&#96;&#96;
</code></pre>

Every chunk after this one, for the rest of the document, will use that
folder as its working directory, regardless of where the `.Rmd` file
itself is saved. Giving this chunk the name `setup` (right after `r` in
the curly braces) isn't required, but it's a strong, widely used
convention, it signals to anyone reading your document that this chunk's
job is configuration, not analysis.

**Try it now:** Add a setup chunk like the one above to the top of your
document, using `getwd()` (from Chapter 6) to check your current working
directory first if you're not sure what path to use. Add a second chunk
below it that just runs `getwd()` again, then knit, and confirm it
reports the folder you set, not the folder your `.Rmd` file is saved in.

**Try it now:** Add a second chunk that connects to the frog database and
computes the average frog weight, this time with `echo=FALSE` so only
the result shows, not the code itself:

<pre><code>&#96;&#96;&#96;{r, echo=FALSE}
library(DBI)
con &lt;- dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "data/frogs.sqlite")
avg_weight &lt;- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT AVG(weight_g) AS avg_weight FROM morphometrics;")
avg_weight
&#96;&#96;&#96;
</code></pre>

Knit again. Notice the code itself doesn't appear this time, only the
number.

### Inline code

Sometimes you want to weave a single computed value directly into a
sentence, rather than displaying it as separate chunk output. **Inline
code** does exactly this, using a single backtick, the letter `r`, your
code, and a closing backtick, right in the middle of regular text.

**Try it now:** Add this sentence to your document body (not inside a
chunk):

```{r, eval=FALSE}
The average frog weight in our dataset is `r round(avg_weight$avg_weight, 1)` grams.
```

(This assumes the `avg_weight` object from the previous chunk has
already run earlier in the document, code chunks execute top to bottom,
in order, just like a script.) Knit the document, and you should see the
actual number appear seamlessly inside the sentence, no separate chunk,
no manual copy-pasting.

### Text formatting

Everything outside of code chunks is plain Markdown text. A few
essentials:

**Headers**, made with one or more `#` symbols, more `#`s for a smaller
heading:

```
# Biggest heading
## Smaller heading
### Even smaller heading
```

**Bold** and *italics*:

```
**this text is bold**
*this text is italic*
```

Bullet lists, using a hyphen and a space:

```
- first item
- second item
- third item
```

Numbered lists, using a number, a period, and a space:

```
1. first step
2. second step
3. third step
```

Links, with the visible text in square brackets immediately followed by
the URL in parentheses:

```
[R Markdown documentation](https://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/)
```

**Try it now:** Add a header, a sentence with one bold word and one
italic word, and a bulleted list of three items to your document. Knit
it, and confirm each renders the way you'd expect.

### Embedding images

To include an existing image file (a photo, a diagram, a logo), use
standard Markdown image syntax:

```
![Alt text describing the image](path/to/image.png)
```

Note that this is different from a plot generated by a code chunk, any
plot your R code produces (with `plot()`, `hist()`, and so on) gets
embedded automatically, with no separate image syntax needed at all, it's
just the natural output of the chunk that created it.

### Adding a table of contents

For longer documents, add a table of contents by adding `toc: true` to
your YAML header, nested under the output format:

```
---
title: "Frog Morphometrics Summary"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
---
```

### Knitting the document

Click the **Knit** button at the top of the source pane (or run
`rmarkdown::render("your-file.Rmd")` from the console) to produce your
final output file. RStudio will show you a preview automatically, and
save the rendered file (an `.html`, in our case) alongside your `.Rmd` in
the same folder.

## In-Class Activity: Building a Frog Data Summary Report

For this activity, you'll build a short RMarkdown report from scratch,
summarizing data from `frogs.sqlite`.

### Setup

1. In RStudio, create a new RMarkdown document (**File > New File > R
   Markdown...**), title it "Frog Data Summary," and select HTML output.
   Delete the example content RStudio generates, keeping only the YAML
   header.

2. Add `toc: true` to your YAML header, nested under `html_document`.

### Your turn

Build a report containing all of the following:

1. **A setup chunk** near the top (using `include=FALSE`, since a reader
   doesn't need to see this) that loads `DBI` and connects to
   `data/frogs.sqlite`.

2. **A section header** ("## Weight Summary"), followed by a chunk (with
   `echo=FALSE`, since only the result matters here) that queries the
   average, minimum, and maximum frog weight from the `morphometrics`
   table, and stores the result in an object.

3. **A sentence using inline code** that reports the average weight
   computed in step 2, woven directly into a sentence (e.g., "Frogs in
   this study weighed an average of *X* grams.").

4. **A second section header** ("## Weight Distribution"), followed by a
   chunk that pulls all weight values from `morphometrics` into R and
   plots a histogram, using base R's `hist()` function:

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   weights <- dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT weight_g FROM morphometrics;")
   hist(weights$weight_g, main = "Frog Weight Distribution", xlab = "Weight (g)")
   ```

5. **Knit your document** to HTML, and confirm the table of contents,
   inline sentence, and histogram all appear correctly.

### What to submit

Submit both your `.Rmd` source file and the knitted `.html` output.
